a: Am I not free?
t: Chapter 9 is not a side trip
p: Paul turns from idol meat to his own life, to show what giving up a right looks like.
b: Chapter 8 ended with Paul ready to give up meat forever rather than make a brother stumble (8:13). Chapter 9 shows that this is what he already does with his rights as an apostle. Some scholars have thought chapter 9 came from another letter, because it seems to stop talking about idol meat. Most now read 8:1-11:1 as one argument. In ancient speeches a speaker often offered his own life as the example to copy, and Paul says so in 11:1: "Be imitators of me." The question "Am I not free?" sets up the whole argument. He is free, so his giving up of rights is a choice.

a: Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?
t: What makes an apostle: seeing the risen Lord
p: Paul counts his sight of the risen Jesus as the same kind of event as Peter's.
b: Paul rests his claim to be an apostle on two things: he has seen the risen Lord, and the Corinthian church is the proof of his work. He lists himself last among those to whom Jesus appeared, "as to one born at the wrong time" (1 Corinthians 15:8, see that chapter), and he describes the event as God revealing his Son to him (Galatians 1:15-16). Luke tells the story as the meeting on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3-6). Some Corinthians doubted his standing because he had not been with Jesus in Galilee, and because he refused their money (9:12). Whether others besides the Twelve can be called apostles is discussed at Romans 16:7 and at 1 Corinthians 15:7.

a: the seal of my apostleship
t: A seal was a stamp of ownership and proof
p: Paul calls the Corinthian church the official stamp that proves his work.
b: A seal (sphragis) was pressed in clay or wax on a document, a jar or a package. It showed who owned it and that it was genuine. Paul says the church itself is the stamp on his claim to be sent by the Lord. Anyone doubting that he is an apostle only needs to look at Corinth, which exists because of his preaching (Acts 18:1-11). The same word appears for God's mark on believers (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13). Paul uses it here about the church as evidence, much as a letter of recommendation would serve (2 Corinthians 3:1-3).

a: a wife who is a believer
p: The Greek says "a sister, a wife." Most read it as a Christian wife; one old view makes the women helpers.
b: The Greek has two nouns side by side, adelphen gynaika, "a sister, a wife." "Sister" here means a Christian woman. Most readers take it as Paul claiming the right to be married and to bring a wife with him at the church's expense, as the other apostles do. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 3.6.53) took it differently: the apostles brought women along as "sisters" who helped in the work, not as wives in the ordinary sense. Clement himself defended marriage, so this was not a plea for celibacy. Jerome (Against Jovinianus 1.26) read the women as devout helpers who, as Jewish custom allowed, supported their teachers with their goods, and he went on to argue that the apostles other than Peter had no wives. Augustine (On the Work of Monks 4.5) likewise says that faithful women went with the apostles and ministered to them of their substance. Paul himself prefers to stay single (7:7-8), but in this verse he defends the right of the other apostles to be married. He does not say whether the wives shared in the work.

a: the Lord's brothers, and Cephas
t: Brothers of the Lord, and a married Peter
p: Paul names the Lord's brothers and Cephas as married apostles; churches differ on who the brothers were.
b: Cephas is Peter, whose mother-in-law Jesus healed (Mark 1:30). The "brothers of the Lord" include James, who led the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13). Who they were is a church question: as Joseph's sons by a first marriage (the Orthodox and older Eastern view), as sons of Joseph and Mary (the view of Helvidius, and of many Protestants), or as cousins (Jerome, followed by Catholic teaching). The topic page lays out each. For this verse, the point is simple: these leaders traveled with wives, and the churches paid for it.

a: stop working for a living
p: Paul and Barnabas earned their own living, which was unusual for traveling teachers.
b: Paul worked with his hands in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, in a trade the book of Acts sums up in these words: "Their craft was making tents" (Acts 18:3). Barnabas worked too; this verse is the only place that says so. A traveling teacher in the Greek world was usually paid by students or supported by a wealthy patron. Paul chose to work in a shop instead. Ronald Hock's study of Paul's tentmaking looks at the trade itself, the workshop as a place to talk about the gospel, and ancient attitudes toward work (The Social Context of Paul's Ministry: Tentmaking and Apostleship, 1980). Manual work also carried low status in Corinth, which makes the choice a deliberate one (4:12; 1 Thessalonians 2:9).

a: serves at his own expense
p: Three ordinary jobs make the point: workers live from their work.
b: Paul starts with three trades every Corinthian knew. A Roman soldier received pay and rations from the state. A vineyard owner ate his own grapes. A shepherd lived on his flock's milk. The word he uses for a soldier's "expense" (opsonion) is the soldier's ration or wage. Corinth was a Roman colony, so the picture was familiar. Paul is not saying the soldier, farmer and shepherd are like apostles in every way. He is saying that no one expects a worker to work with nothing in return. Then he turns to Scripture (9:8-10) and to the temple (9:13).

a: You shall not muzzle an ox that is treading out the grain.
t: Deuteronomy 25:4: Do not muzzle the ox
p: Paul reads a law about oxen as a rule for paying those who work, and asks if God cares only about oxen.
b: This is Deuteronomy 25:4, which this site's Plain reads: "Do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing." The Hebrew pictures an ox pulling a threshing sledge over the grain. Paul's word for "muzzle" (kemoo) is rare; the Greek Old Testament uses a different word (phimoo), and the Byzantine copyists changed Paul to match it. His question, "Is it oxen that God cares about?" does not deny God's care for animals. Philo (On the Virtues 145) praises this law as part of Moses' kindness to animals. Paul's own point is an argument from lesser to greater: if the law protects the ox, how much more the one who labors for people. The same verse is quoted in 1 Timothy 5:18 beside a saying of Jesus.

a: Yes, it was written for our sake.
t: Does the law speak about oxen or about us?
p: Paul says the law was written for the church's sake, a way of reading that Jews and Christians still discuss.
b: Paul's "for our sake" is a claim about how to read the law of Moses: it was written with later readers in view. Paul's words mean that he reads Scripture as addressed to the church of his day, which is why he can use a small rule about an ox. Others call this allegory, a reading that looks past the plain sense of a verse. Paul does not drop the plain sense here: oxen are protected, and by the same reasoning, workers. Many Jewish teachers also reasoned from a small rule of Torah to a wider principle (the method called qal vahomer, "light and heavy"). Paul's reasoning in 9:9-10 is that kind of argument.

a: we have not used this right
p: Taking pay from a rich Corinthian could have made Paul that person's dependent.
b: The reason Paul will not take money from Corinth is not that supporting a preacher is wrong; verses 4-14 argue the opposite. In a city built on patronage, accepting a rich man's gift meant becoming his client and owing him loyalty and public praise. Refusing a rich man's gift could look like refusing the friendship he was offering, and this may lie behind some of the hostility Paul faces (2 Corinthians 11:7-11; 12:13-16). Peter Marshall's Enmity in Corinth: Social Conventions in Paul's Relations with the Corinthians (1987) studies the conventions of friendship and enmity behind Paul's relations with the Corinthians. Paul did accept help from the Philippians, who were not in a position to claim anything from him (Philippians 4:15-16).

a: those who attend the altar have their share from the altar
p: The law gave priests and Levites a share of the offerings; Paul compares his preaching to that.
b: Under the law of Moses the priests and Levites received portions of the offerings and the tithes (Numbers 18:8-32; Deuteronomy 18:1-5). They owned no land in Israel, and God's service was their livelihood. Paul says the same principle supports those who announce the good news. Pagan temples also fed their staff from sacrifices, so Gentile Corinthians would have understood the picture too. The word "temple" here is general ("sacred things"), and Paul may be thinking of both. He will use the altar in a very different way in 10:18-21, where eating at an idol's altar makes one a partner of what the altar serves.

a: the Lord gave an order
t: A saying of Jesus behind Paul's argument
p: Paul probably has in mind Jesus' instruction to the Twelve and the Seventy about being fed by those they serve.
b: Paul does not say where the Lord gave this order. The closest sayings are in the missions of the Twelve and of the seventy-two. This site's Plain reads, "A worker has earned his food" (Matthew 10:10), and, "for a worker has earned his pay" (Luke 10:7). Paul's wording is his own, and he shows that he knows a tradition of Jesus' sayings and treats it as binding (compare 7:10 and 11:23). He says the Lord "gave an order," not just that this is wise. That makes his refusal of pay his own free choice, not obedience to a command.

a: make my boast empty
p: Paul's Greek stops in mid-sentence, as if too moved to finish.
b: The Greek of 9:15 does not finish properly. It says, roughly, "it would be better for me to die than-- no one will make my boast empty." Scribes tried to repair it: the Byzantine copyists wrote "than that anyone should make my boast empty," which is the smoother reading behind the KJV (see the variant). Paul's "boast" (kauchema) is what he proudly holds on to: that he preaches free of charge. Boasting is usually bad in Paul (1:29, 31), so he is careful here to say what the boast rests on, that he gives the good news away.

a: a necessity is laid on me
p: Paul describes his call in the words of the prophets: he cannot keep quiet.
b: Paul says he has no right to boast of preaching, because it is not his choice: "a necessity is laid on me," and "woe" to him if he does not do it. The picture is prophetic. Jeremiah said that God's word was like a fire shut up in his bones and he could not hold it in (Jeremiah 20:9). Amos said that when the Lord speaks, who can refuse to prophesy (Amos 3:8). Paul elsewhere describes his call in prophetic terms, as set apart before birth (Galatians 1:15-16, compare Jeremiah 1:5). Here the compulsion explains why he cannot expect a reward for what he must do, and why what he can offer is something extra: preaching for free.

a: What, then, is my reward?
t: A reward for what he cannot help doing?
p: Verses 17-18 are hard: Paul says he is compelled, yet looks for a reward in giving the good news free.
b: Paul's logic in 9:17-18 has puzzled readers. If he does it willingly, he has a reward. If unwillingly, he is still a steward entrusted with a task. Then he asks what his reward is, and answers that it is the freedom to give the good news away for nothing. Commentators read this in two main ways. One: his compulsion is real, so wages are not what he is owed; his only "reward" is the privilege of preaching without charge. Two: he is playing on two meanings of "reward," a wage owed to a free worker and a prize awarded to one who goes beyond duty. Either way the point is the same: he gives up his rights as an apostle by choice.

a: I made myself everyone's slave
t: Free, yet a slave to all
p: A free man who chooses slavery for others' sake turns Roman values upside down.
b: In Roman Corinth a free person's whole standing rested on not being a slave. Paul says he is free from everyone, then "made myself everyone's slave." The Greek word is the verb of doulos, "slave," the same family as in Romans 1:1. Dale Martin's Slavery as Salvation (1990) studies Paul's slavery language for leaders. The words would still have jarred a status-conscious church. They are not a plan for how to get people to follow him. His point is that his freedom is the very thing he gives up.

a: To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win Jews.
t: Paul, the Torah and becoming "like a Jew"
p: Did Paul keep the law with Jews? Scholars answer in three ways, and Jewish scholars take part in the debate.
b: Paul says he became "like a Jew" for Jews, and "like one under the law" for those under the law, "though I am not myself under the law." Three readings are common. (1) Paul stayed a Torah-observant Jew and never required Gentile believers to become Jews (David Rudolph, A Jew to the Jews, reads 9:19-23 together with 10:32-11:1 and argues that it does not show Paul gave up the law). On this view "becoming like" is about how he shared meals and lived among others, not a break with the law. Acts 16:3 and 21:23-26 show him acting as an observant Jew. (2) Paul no longer saw the law as binding on himself, and took on its practices only for the sake of mission. Reviewers of Rudolph's book say it has not overturned this second reading. (3) The charge of pretending is old: Jerome read the similar scene in Galatians 2 as a staged pretense by Peter and Paul, and Augustine rejected that as making the apostles liars. That is an ancient charge about Galatians 2, and no modern holder of it is named here. The Byzantine text lacks the clause "though I am not myself under the law" (see the variant).

a: under Christ's law
t: "Christ's law" and the people "outside the law"
p: "Outside the law" means Gentiles, not lawless people. "Christ's law" has several readings.
b: "Those outside the law" (anomoi) are Gentiles, people without the Torah; it does not mean wicked people. Paul says he is not outside "God's law" but "under Christ's law" (ennomos Christou). He uses the phrase again in Galatians 6:2, "the law of Christ." It has been read as: the teaching and example of Jesus; the Torah as read through the love command; a new law replacing Moses (an older Protestant and Catholic reading, each with its own sense); or Paul's way of saying he is bound to Christ and not free from obligation. The Plain keeps the literal "Christ's law."

a: on a race course everyone runs
p: Corinth hosted one of the great games of Greece, and Paul's readers would have known its runners and boxers.
b: The Isthmian Games were held every two years at the sanctuary of Poseidon on the isthmus, a few miles from Corinth, and the city ran them in Paul's day. Events included foot races, boxing, wrestling and chariot racing. Acts 18:11 says Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half. The winner's crown in this period was a wreath of pine or celery; the sources are not fully agreed. Paul uses the contest as a picture of discipline, and he leaves behind the rule "only one wins": he wants all the Corinthians to run to win ("Run in a way that you can win it").

a: a crown that fades
p: The words for a fading wreath and one that never fades return in chapter 15.
b: The wreath was green leaves, so it withered within days. Paul sets "perishable" (phthartos) against "imperishable" (aphthartos), two words he will use again for the resurrection body: what is sown perishable is raised imperishable (15:42), and the perishable must put on the imperishable (15:53; see that chapter). The self-control (enkrateuetai) of the athlete is a daily training for something that lasts. Other writers use the crown for martyrs and faithful servants (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4; James 1:12).

a: am disqualified myself
p: The Greek word means failing a test. Churches read it as losing a prize, a ministry or salvation.
b: The word is adokimos, the opposite of "approved": a coin that fails the assayer's test, a runner who breaks the rules. The KJV has "castaway." What is Paul afraid of? (1) Losing the reward or his place in service, while remaining saved (many Reformed and Baptist teachers). (2) Losing salvation itself (Wesleyan and Pentecostal readings, and the Catholic and Orthodox sense that a believer can fall by grave sin). (3) A rhetorical warning to the strong in Corinth, who thought their knowledge and rituals made them safe (10:1-12 supports this). The card on this chapter gives each church's own words. Verse 10:12 repeats the warning.

a: our fathers
t: "Our fathers": Paul writes to Gentiles about Israel's story
p: Most of the Corinthians were not Jews, yet Paul calls Israel in the wilderness "our fathers."
b: The church at Corinth was mostly Gentile (12:2: "when you were Gentiles"). Paul still says "our fathers." He may be speaking as a Jew, though the "our" sits oddly with his readers. More likely he means that Gentile believers have been brought into Israel's story through the Messiah (Romans 4:11-12, 16-17; 11:17-24; Galatians 3:29). Some interpreters read the whole of chapter 10 this way: Scripture is the church's own family history. Others, including readers in the Paul-within-Judaism school, stress that the Gentiles are not turned into Jews, but are drawn into Israel's God and Israel's Scripture as Gentiles. Either way, the wilderness generation is not someone else's story.

a: baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea
p: Paul sees the exodus as a baptism that bound Israel to its leader, as baptism binds believers to Christ.
b: The cloud and the sea belong to the exodus: "The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground" (Exodus 14:22), with the pillar of cloud over them (Exodus 13:21; 14:19-20). Paul says they were "baptized into Moses," bound to him as leader as Christians are "baptized into Christ" (Romans 6:3; Galatians 3:27; 1 Corinthians 12:13, see that chapter). The word is a one-time image: no one is said to have been dipped in water. Tertullian (On Baptism 9) read the crossing of the sea, with its water, as a picture of Christian baptism. The Greek verb is passive in NA28 and middle ("had themselves baptized") in the SBL and Byzantine text; the English is the same either way.

a: the same spiritual food
t: Spiritual: from the Spirit, not unreal
p: "Spiritual" here means given by God's Spirit. The manna and the water were real food and drink.
b: The manna (Exodus 16:15, where the Israelites asked "What is it?") and the water from the rock are meant. "Spiritual" (pneumatikos) in Paul does not mean "not physical"; it means belonging to or given by the Spirit (compare 2:13-15, 12:1). The word "same" stresses that every one of them received it, with no difference between the privileged and the rest. That is the point of verses 1-5: all had the same gifts, yet most were struck down. Many fathers heard the Lord's Supper behind the food and drink (see the card on 10:16), but Paul himself does not say so.

a: that rock was the Christ
t: The rock that went with them
p: Paul says Christ was the rock in the wilderness. Jewish stories of a traveling rock or well lie behind the idea.
b: Exodus tells of water from the rock at Horeb: "You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it" (Exodus 17:6, God speaking to Moses). Numbers 20:11 tells of a second rock at Kadesh. Philo took the rock as a symbol of God's wisdom (Allegorical Interpretation 2.86). Paul says the rock was the Christ. Readers have taken this as: Christ was truly present with Israel; the rock stands for Christ as a pattern (typology); or Paul is speaking of Christ as God's Wisdom, which he calls Christ elsewhere (1:24, 30; 8:6). The Plain has "the Christ" as the Greek has the article.

a: became examples for us
t: Types: patterns pressed into a mold
p: The Greek word is the root of "typology." It means a pattern or model, and here a moral warning.
b: Typos began as the mark left by a blow, then a mold or stamp, then a pattern or model. In 10:6 and 10:11 Paul uses it for events in Israel's past that give the church a pattern to avoid: craving, idol feasts, sexual sin, testing God and grumbling. Leonhard Goppelt's Typos: The Typological Interpretation of the Old Testament in the New studies this "typological" way of reading. Paul does not say these events predicted the church, only that they happened "to them" and were written down for us. The "evil things" they craved echo the "graves of craving" in Numbers 11:4, 34. The same word is in Romans 5:14 (Adam as a type of the one to come).

a: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
p: Paul quotes Exodus 32:6, the feast at the golden calf, as a warning about idol banquets in Corinth.
b: This site's Plain of Exodus 32:6 reads, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and they got up to play." Paul quotes the Greek Old Testament almost word for word. In Exodus it is the meal after offerings to the golden calf. "Play" (the Hebrew verb is tsachaq) covers dancing and revelry, and in Genesis 26:8 it is used of Isaac and Rebekah's caressing. Paul's word for idolater (eidololatres) is the one he used at 5:10-11, and in 8:10 he pictured a Corinthian eating in an idol's temple. The warning is aimed at the dinner-club banquets in pagan temples.

a: twenty-three thousand fell in one day
p: Numbers 25:9 says 24,000 died. Paul says 23,000. Readers explain the difference in three ways.
b: This site's Plain of Numbers 25:9 reads, "Those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand." The story is that Israel joined in the sex and sacrifices of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1-9). Paul gives 23,000 and adds "in one day," which Numbers does not say. Three explanations are common. (1) The two numbers count different things. Numbers 25:4-5 also tells of leaders who were put to death, so one old harmonizing view is that the 24,000 includes about a thousand leaders executed, leaving 23,000 who fell by the plague; another is that Paul counts only those who died on a single day. (2) Paul is giving the number loosely or in round numbers, and the exact figure does not matter to his warning. (3) The difference is real and not settled, and Paul's point, a mass death in a day, does not depend on the count. Hebrew Numbers 25:9 and the Greek translation both give 24,000 in the editions used here. The editions on this site print 23,000 in 1 Corinthians 10:8 with no variant. The Plain follows Paul's Greek. Exodus 32:28 gives a different figure, 3,000, for the golden calf, so the two stories should not be mixed.

a: the Destroyer
p: Paul's "Destroyer" is God's agent of death, named in Exodus and the grumbling stories.
b: The Destroyer (ho olothreutes) is the one who struck Egypt's firstborn on the night of Passover. This site's Plain reads, "He will not let the destroyer come into your houses to strike you" (Exodus 12:23). Wisdom of Solomon 18:25 also speaks of "the destroyer." Paul puts the title on the plague after the grumbling in the wilderness, perhaps the plague after Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:41-49) or the snakes of Numbers 21. Is this an angel, a spirit or God himself at work? The Old Testament often leaves it open; Paul only says Israel was destroyed by it. Hebrews 11:28 uses the same root (olothreuo), as the participle "the destroyer."
r: Exodus 12:23; Numbers 16:41-49; Wisdom of Solomon 18:25; Hebrews 11:28

a: the ends of the ages have come
p: Paul says the church lives where two ages overlap.
b: The Greek says "the ends" (plural, ta tele) "of the ages." Paul thinks the history of Israel runs in ages, and that the final age has already begun with the Messiah's death and resurrection, although the old age has not finished (15:20-28; Galatians 1:4; 4:4). Some commentators say the church stands where the last age meets the present one, others that "ends" means goals or fulfillments. Paul uses this to turn the exodus story into a warning for the church: having arrived at the final stage of the story is no protection.

a: You have faced only the kind of testing that people face.
t: Testing or temptation? And "more than you can handle"
p: The Greek word means both. The verse is about idol feasts, not about suffering in general.
b: Peirasmos means both "test" and "temptation": a trial of what you are made of, or a pull toward sin. Here it is a test of loyalty to God in Corinth's temple meals and idol feasts (10:14), so the way out is to leave. A popular saying, "God won't give you more than you can handle," comes from this verse, but it is not what Paul says. He speaks of a test, not a disaster; he promises that God sets limits to testing; and Paul can say elsewhere that he was under pressure "beyond our strength" (2 Corinthians 1:8). The "way out" (ekbasis) is a word for an exit, such as a path out of a narrow pass, and the promise is that God provides an escape, not that the test is easy.

a: a sharing in the blood of Christ
p: Paul's word means joint participation. What it means in the Lord's Supper is a main church debate.
b: Koinonia is "sharing, partnership, fellowship." Paul asks whether the cup and bread are a sharing in Christ's blood and body, and he expects the answer yes. He does not say how. The "cup of blessing" is the cup over which a blessing is said. Some link it to the third cup of the Passover meal, over which, in the Mishnah (Pesachim 10:7), the blessing after the meal is said. The Last Supper may be in view (11:25), but the Mishnah was written down long after Paul, so the link is a possibility, not a certainty. The Greek has "the blood" before "the body," the reverse of 11:24-25, and "body" has a double sense here, as 10:17 shows: the body of Christ and the church. The card below sets out how the churches read it. The same word returns in 10:18, 20, where eating at an altar makes a person a partner of the altar's god.

a: we who are many are one body
p: The loaf is a picture of unity. Paul turns "the body of Christ" from the bread to the church.
b: Paul slides from Christ's body in the bread (10:16) to the church as one body made by sharing it. The Didache (9:4), an early church manual, has a prayer over the broken bread that builds on the same image: as this broken bread was once scattered over the hills and, gathered, became one, so may the church be gathered into one from the ends of the earth. The idea matters for Corinth. The strong, who feel free to eat anywhere, are cutting the one body in pieces when they eat in idol temples, and the rich who eat first are doing the same at the Lord's table (11:21). Chapter 12 develops the body fully.

a: Look at Israel according to the flesh.
p: Paul means the people Israel as an earthly nation. It does not mean the church replaced it.
b: "According to the flesh" here means in its ordinary, outward, ethnic sense: the people of Israel as a historical nation, whose priests ate from the altar in Jerusalem. Paul does not use the phrase to cast Israel aside. He uses Israel's sacrifices as a plain example of a principle (eating from an altar means sharing in it) that applies in the temples of Corinth. The same ethnic sense of "flesh" is in Romans 9:3, 5. Some ancient readers took "according to the flesh" in contrast to a "spiritual Israel"; Paul's phrasing does not require that, and this verse is better kept apart from the later use of the contrast. Compare Galatians 6:16.

a: they sacrifice to demons and not to God
p: Paul echoes the Song of Moses. Idols are nothing, but what lies behind them is not harmless.
b: Paul takes the words from Deuteronomy 32:17, which this site's Plain reads, "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God." In 8:4 Paul agreed that "an idol is nothing" and "there is no God but one." Here he adds that the sacrifices are not nothing: they go to demons. The Jewish tradition had the same two ideas, that idols are empty and that spirits can use them (Psalm 106:37; Baruch 4:7). He does not say the meat is changed, only that sharing a table with demons makes the diner their partner. The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which has no "the Gentiles" here (see the variant).

a: the table of the Lord and the table of demons
t: Two tables: dinners in a temple
p: Temple dining rooms in Corinth hosted ordinary parties, and Paul says a believer cannot sit at both tables.
b: Diners in a Greek temple reclined in side rooms to eat meat from sacrifices, often under the name of the god. A papyrus invitation from Egypt asks a guest "to dine at the couch of the lord Sarapis" (deipnesai eis kleinen tou kyriou Sarapidos; P.Oxy. 1.110, second century). The Greek says "couch," though English versions often give "table"; the dining couch stands for the banquet. Paul had already pictured such a meal in 8:10. Here he says that a person cannot take the Lord's cup and also share in this meal, because each makes the diner a partner of someone. The line he draws is between sharing in a temple banquet and eating idol-meat bought in a market (10:25) or served in a home (10:27). Alex Cheung (Idol Food in Corinth) and Peter Gooch (Dangerous Food) each wrote a book on the subject.

a: making the Lord jealous
p: This echoes the Song of Moses: God is jealous when Israel turns to other gods.
b: The Song of Moses runs from sacrifices to demons (Deuteronomy 32:17) to God's jealousy: Israel made him jealous with what is no god (Deuteronomy 32:21). Paul echoes the idea and asks whether the Corinthians want to test it. God's "jealousy" in the Old Testament is his claim on an exclusive love, like a husband's (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). The question "Are we stronger than he is?" is the question that Israel's own history answers (10:5-10).

a: "Everything is lawful,"
t: A Corinthian slogan, answered a second time
p: Paul probably quotes the Corinthians' own slogan and limits it.
b: "Everything is lawful" was said already at 6:12, where Paul answers "but not everything is helpful." Most commentators think it is a slogan of the strong in Corinth, maybe a distortion of Paul's own teaching about freedom, that Paul quotes and then limits. Not all agree: some think Paul is the origin of the phrase and means it. In 10:23 the limits are "helpful" and "builds up" (a key word for Paul; 8:1), which is where the argument is headed: freedom matters, but love for others sets the rule. The words "for me" are in the Byzantine text and in 6:12; the SBLGNT has none here.

a: Eat anything that is sold in the meat market
p: Much meat for sale came from temple sacrifices. Paul says a believer need not ask.
b: Corinth's market (makellon) sold meat that had been through the temples, because priests sold what the altar did not use. A visitor could not easily tell where a cut had come from. A Jewish person would ask; Paul tells the Corinthians not to. Paul's rule is that the meat is not changed by the sacrifice, because "the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord" (10:26). A Jewish Christian who kept the food laws would still have to ask about other things (the meat's kosher status), which is why this rule is for the Gentile majority. The Apostolic Decree of Acts 15:29 told Gentile believers to avoid food offered to idols, and churches have read that as still in force or as limited in time (see the card).

a: the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord
p: Paul quotes Psalm 24:1: all food belongs to God, so no idol can claim it.
b: This site's Plain of Psalm 24:1 reads, "To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it, / the world and those who live there." Paul uses the first half as a reason that the meat in the market is clean. The psalm puts the whole earth in the Lord's hands; no idol owns even a piece of meat. Jewish blessings over food use the same idea (the blessing over bread thanks the one who brings forth bread from the earth). Paul has "the Lord" where the Hebrew has the divine name; in 10:21, "the cup of the Lord" has Christ in view. Some Byzantine copies repeat the quotation in 10:28 (see the variant).

a: is from a sacrifice
p: The word Paul puts in the host's mouth is polite. The rest of the book calls it idol food.
b: The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which has hierothyton ("offered in a holy rite"). This is how a pagan host would say it. Elsewhere in chapters 8-10, Paul says eidolothyton ("idol-sacrifice"), the Jewish term. The Byzantine copyists changed the word in 10:28 to match (see the variant). Who is the informer? Probably a pagan guest or host, who thinks the Christian would care; or a weak believer. In either case the rule is that the meat is not the issue. What matters is what eating it says to the one who told you, "for the sake of the one who told you."

a: I mean the other person's conscience, not your own.
p: The conscience in question belongs to the one who raised it. Paul's own freedom is not up for a vote.
b: Syneidesis is "conscience," literally a "knowing along with oneself" that judges one's own acts (Romans 2:15; 9:1). Here Paul is not asking the strong to sacrifice their own conscience; he asks them to protect the other person's. The question "why is my freedom judged by someone else's conscience?" is possibly the strong's reply, or Paul's own words: if I am free in thanks to God, why let another judge me? He answers it by 10:31-33. The flexibility is hard to hold: a Christian is free, yet cannot use freedom to wound.

a: If I eat with thanks
p: The Greek word is charis, which can mean thanks or grace.
b: Paul writes chariti, the dative of charis, which means "grace" and also "thanks." The KJV has "by grace": if I share in the meal as a gift of God. Most translators take it as thanks, because the next clause says "something I give thanks for" (eucharisto), and the Plain follows them. The two senses are close for Paul, who thinks of food as a gift received with thanks (compare 10:26 and 1 Timothy 4:3-5). His point is that a believer who eats with thanks to God should not be condemned for it, but he goes on to say that this freedom is limited by love (10:31-33).

a: do everything for the glory of God
p: Eating, drinking and everything else is to be done for God's glory.
b: Paul ends the long argument with a rule that does not depend on any one case: eat, drink, do anything, for God's glory. Everything in chapters 8-10 is an application of that principle: freedom that serves God does not make others fall, and it does not take part in anything given to a rival. Paul's Jewish background supplies the idea that an ordinary meal can be an act of worship: the blessing before and after the meal is part of it (compare 10:30, "with thanks"). Colossians 3:17 puts it the same way.

a: Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God
t: Three groups: Jews, Greeks, the church
p: Paul lists the three groups he must not offend. "Greek" means non-Jew.
b: Paul speaks of three groups: Jews, Greeks and "the church of God." "Greek" here means a Gentile of any nation. Paul usually divides humanity into Jew and Greek (1:22-24; 12:13). By naming the church as a third group he already sees it as a distinct people, drawn from both. The command not to give offense fits his own practice in 9:19-23, where he moves among Jews, those under the law and those outside it. He closes with himself as the model, as in 11:1.

a: so that they may be saved
p: Paul says he pleases everyone, which sounds like flattery. He means he looks to their benefit, not his own.
b: "Please everyone in everything" is not people-pleasing for its own sake. Paul says in Galatians 1:10 that if he were still trying to please people, he would not be a slave of Christ. He means taking others' good as his aim (10:24), the opposite of the "it's lawful for me" attitude. The purpose clause gives the goal: "so that they may be saved." This is the same goal as in 9:22. It sums up the whole of 8:1-10:33: knowledge puffs up, but love builds up, and love looks to the salvation of others.

a: the traditions
p: Paul's word is "traditions," things received and passed on. It is not a bad word for him.
b: The Greek is paradoseis, "things handed on," from the verb used in 11:23 ("I handed on to you") and 15:3. Paul is a link in a chain: he received something and passes it on. Here the teachings are the practices and sayings he gave the church, which may include the matters of worship that follow. The word is behind the church debate on "Scripture and tradition," in which Catholic and Orthodox teachers appeal to 11:2 and 2 Thessalonians 2:15, and Protestant teachers reply that the teachings Paul meant are those now in the New Testament. Paul himself says only that the Corinthians are to hold them. The Plain says "traditions," as it does in Galatians 1:14 and in Mark 7:8-9, so the reader can see that the Greek word is the same whether Paul praises it here or Jesus criticizes it there. The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which has no "brothers" here (see the variant).

a: But I want you to know that
p: The passage has more disputed points than any other in the letter. Here is what they are.
b: This passage is hard for five reasons. (1) The word kephale, "head," can mean the top of the body, a source, or a ruler (note at 11:3). (2) Greek has one word for "man" and "husband," and one for "woman" and "wife" (note at 11:3). (3) It is unclear what the covering was: a veil, a shawl, or the arrangement of the hair (note at 11:4). (4) "Authority on her head" (11:10) and "because of the angels" are cryptic. (5) Paul seems to allow women to pray and prophesy aloud (11:5), yet 14:34-35 tells women to be silent. Some scholars have asked whether 11:2-16, or 11:3-16, was added by a later hand, but that view has not persuaded many. All the early manuscripts have it.

a: the head of a woman is the man
p: "Head" may mean source, ruler or prominent part, and "man/woman" may mean "husband/wife."
b: Kephale ("head") has three main readings here. Authority: the head rules, as in Ephesians 5:23. Source: the head is origin, as in 11:8, "woman from man," and Christ is the source of every man, as in the creation of all things. Prominence: the head is the visible top or leading part. Joseph Fitzmyer's "Another Look at Kephale in 1 Corinthians 11.3" (New Testament Studies 35, 1989) concludes that a Greek-speaking Jewish writer like Paul could well have meant "head" as authority over someone, the first reading. The order in the verse is Christ, man, God, then Christ again: it is not a straight ladder. Aner and gyne mean "man" and "woman" or "husband" and "wife"; the Plain uses "man" and "woman" and leaves the choice to the reader, because 11:11-12 speaks of men and women generally. Each reading changes what "headship" means.

a: something hanging down from his head
p: Paul's Greek says only "down from the head." It may mean a veil, a shawl, or long hair.
b: The Greek is kata kephales echon, "having down from the head." Richard Oster's article "When Men Wore Veils to Worship: The Historical Context of 1 Corinthians 11.4" (New Testament Studies 34, 1988) sets the verse in the Roman practice of men veiling in worship. Others think the issue was hair: men wearing long hair, or women with loose hair, which could carry sexual meaning. Still others read it against the dress of the respectable Roman woman. Reading these customs back into Corinth is risky.

a: prays or prophesies with her head uncovered
t: Women who pray and prophesy aloud
p: Paul assumes women speak to God and for God in the assembly. 14:34-35 seems to say the opposite.
b: Paul takes for granted that women "pray or prophesy" in the church's meeting; his only concern is how they do it. Prophesying is speaking God's word to the congregation (14:3). The tension with 14:34-35 has been settled in several ways: (1) 14:34-35 is about one kind of speech, such as weighing the prophets' words. (2) Paul here corrects only one fault and takes up women's speaking later, in chapter 14. (3) 14:34-35 is a later addition, in which case 11:5 is Paul's real view. (4) Antoinette Clark Wire's The Corinthian Women Prophets: A Reconstruction through Paul's Rhetoric (1990) reads Paul's arguments in 1 Corinthians for evidence of the women prophets he is answering. The card on 11:2-16 gives each church's practice.

a: have her hair cropped
t: Shaved or cropped: why it was shameful
p: A woman with shaved or cropped hair in Corinth marked herself as a particular kind of person.
b: In Paul's world a woman's cropped or shaved head could suggest a woman convicted of adultery, a slave, a woman in mourning, or someone who rejected women's roles. Paul's argument is a play on shame: if she will not cover her head, she may as well cut her hair, but that would be shameful, so she should cover it. The word translated "cropped" (keiro) means cut short; "shaved" is a stronger word. Neither is a word for what is normal.

a: the image and glory of God
t: Image of God and glory of man
p: Paul echoes Genesis 1:27, but calls only the man God's "image and glory." Many readers find this odd.
b: This site's Plain of Genesis 1:27 reads, "So God created the human in his image, / in God's image he created him, / male and female he created them." Paul says the man is "the image and glory of God" and the woman is "the glory of man." He does not say that woman is not in God's image; other readers point out that Genesis 1:27 says both were, and that Paul must know it (compare Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:10). Some say Paul is arguing from Genesis 2 (woman from man), not Genesis 1. Others say he gives a different sense: "glory" as reflecting honor. All the major Christian traditions teach that men and women are both made in God's image (see, for example, Catechism 369-372).

a: woman from man
t: The order of creation in Genesis 2
p: Paul uses the story of Eve's creation from Adam's rib and then qualifies it in 11:11-12.
b: This site's Plain of Genesis 2:23 reads, "This one at last is bone from my bones / and flesh from my flesh." Paul uses the order of creation (woman from man) and the purpose (woman for man) as arguments for the covering. Then in 11:11-12 he turns: in the Lord, neither is without the other, and man comes through woman. The question for readers is whether the order of creation sets a lasting rule or serves only as one argument in a local matter. The Genesis text does not use the word "head" or give a ranking, as Paul's argument seems to. The church debate is gathered on the card for this section.

a: authority on her head
p: Whose authority? Hers, her husband's, or the veil as a sign? Scholars have proposed all three.
b: The Greek says a woman ought to have exousia ("authority" or "right") on her head. The KJV has "power on her head," and some versions say "a sign of authority," which the Greek does not say. Possible readings: (1) her own authority or right to pray and prophesy, symbolized by the covering (Morna Hooker's "Authority on Her Head: An Examination of 1 Cor. XI.10," New Testament Studies 10, 1963-64, objects that it gives exousia a strange meaning to take the covering as a sign of subjection); (2) the covering is a sign that she is under her husband's authority, the older and still common reading; (3) she has authority over her own head, to decide how to dress, and should use it for the sake of order. The question is still open.
orig: ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς (exousian echein epi tes kephales)

a: because of the angels
p: No one is sure what the angels have to do with it. Readers have proposed several answers.
b: Proposals: (1) Angels as guardians of order in worship, who are offended by disorder. Joseph Fitzmyer compared the angels of 11:10 with the Dead Sea Scrolls, whose community held that holy angels were present at its gatherings ("A Feature of Qumran Angelology and the Angels of 1 Cor. 11:10," New Testament Studies 4, 1957-58). (2) The fallen angels of Genesis 6:1-4 who desired women, so that a woman's head must be covered not to tempt them (Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins 7, took this view). (3) Good angels as witnesses of the church's order, as in Paul's other uses (1 Corinthians 4:9; 6:3; Ephesians 3:10). (4) "Angels" means human messengers or visitors. (5) The phrase is a later insertion. Each has defenders. None is certain.

a: in the Lord, woman is not apart from man
t: "In the Lord": the turn in the argument
p: After the order of creation, Paul says men and women depend on each other in the Lord.
b: "Still" (plen) turns the argument. In the Lord's new age, men and women are mutually dependent. The statement, with 11:12 ("man comes through woman"), balances what comes before. For many egalitarian readers, this reveals Paul's real view and makes the earlier verses a response to a local problem. Complementarian readers say 11:11-12 qualifies but does not cancel the order. Catholic and Orthodox teaching stresses the equal dignity of the two sexes (Catechism 369-372). The reading of the whole passage often depends on how much weight 11:11-12 gets.

a: Does not even nature itself teach you
p: By "nature" Paul probably means the sense of what is fitting in his culture, as Stoics used the word.
b: Physis is "nature." Paul uses it for what the world teaches by its ordinary order. In his day long hair on a man was seen as unmanly, but not everywhere. Long hair on a man was not shameful everywhere: Herodotus (7.208) pictures Spartan soldiers combing their hair before battle, and Nazirites let it grow (Numbers 6:5). Greek philosophers were known for their beards, not for long hair. Many readers hold that Paul means what was seen as fitting in Corinth, not a law of biology (the same word in Romans 1:26 is debated). The question "Does nature teach you" is rhetorical, an appeal to common sense. Paul's own practice shows that custom matters in his argument: 11:16 closes with "we have no such custom."

a: in place of a covering
p: Does the verse say hair is the covering, so nothing more is needed? Or that hair is given as a model for the veil?
b: The Greek word anti can mean "in place of" or "corresponding to." If "in place of," Paul's point is that her long hair is itself the covering, and he has been arguing about hair. If "corresponding to," then the hair is a kind of natural veil and shows that a cloth covering fits. Hair-as-covering is the reading of those who take the whole passage to be about hairstyles. The covering-as-cloth reading is the traditional one, found in the early church (Tertullian) and in the Catholic and Orthodox practice. There is an obvious objection to the hair-only reading: if her hair is already the covering, verse 6 ("if a woman will not cover herself, let her also have her hair cropped") says in effect "if she will not have hair, let her cut her hair." Readers who find a cloth in verses 4-7 point to this. The word here, peribolaion, means a wrap or mantle, and it is not the word of verses 4-7 (katakalypto, "cover"). The Plain keeps "in place of," and that choice leans toward the hair reading; a translator who took anti as "corresponding to" would lean toward the cloth. The question is left open.

a: we have no such custom
p: Paul ends the argument with an appeal to custom. Which custom does he mean?
b: Paul closes with a sharp turn: if anyone wants to argue, "we have no such custom, and neither do the churches of God." What custom? (1) The custom of arguing: Paul and the churches do not allow contentiousness. (2) The custom of women praying uncovered. (3) The custom of men or women acting with no regard for the order he has just given. (4) "We have no other practice" than the one he has just described, that is, covering; this is the sense many modern translations give. Which reading is right depends on how the whole passage is read. The sentence also shows that Paul thinks churches share practices, a theme in 4:17, 7:17 and 14:33.

a: I cannot praise you
t: Corinthian meals: the setting of the Supper
p: Early Christians met in homes for a shared meal. The rich arrived first and ate better.
b: The church met in houses, probably of the larger homes of its wealthier members (Gaius hosted "the whole church," Romans 16:23). A typical Roman villa's dining room held about nine people reclining, with the atrium holding perhaps thirty to forty. The overflow would sit outside, and better guests might be placed in the dining room with better food. One common reconstruction is that the Supper became a social collision between rich who had leisure and food, and poor who came after work with nothing. This fits Paul's complaint that "each person takes his own supper ahead of the rest" (11:21). The Lord's Supper in this setting is a full meal with the bread at its start and the cup at its end (11:25).

a: There have to be factions among you
p: Paul seems to say divisions are needed to show who is genuine. Readers take this as irony or as an end-time pattern.
b: Haireseis ("factions") is the root of "heresy." In Paul it means parties that cut across the church, not false teaching alone (compare Galatians 5:20). "There have to be" (dei) uses a word that speaks of divine necessity. Some commentators read it as Paul's grim irony: you will have them, and God can use them to show who stands the test. Others see an end-time pattern in which the last days bring division (compare Matthew 24:10-12; 1 John 2:19). Still others read "approved" (dokimoi) as those who pass a test, and the factions as the test. The sense in all views is that divisions expose character.

a: what you are eating is not the Lord's Supper
t: "The Lord's Supper": the only use in the Bible
p: This is the only place in the New Testament where the meal is called "the Lord's supper."
b: The phrase kyriakon deipnon ("the Lord's meal") occurs only here. "Supper" (deipnon) means the main evening meal. The Corinthians were holding a full meal in which the rich ate first, so what was meant to be the Lord's was their own. The Greek can also be read "it is not possible to eat the Lord's supper" (the KJV has "this is not to eat the Lord's supper"). The Plain takes the usual sense. Paul does not say it is not a true Lord's Supper in a ritual sense; he says it is not Lord-like in character. Churches use different names: "the Lord's Supper" (Reformed, Baptist and others), "the Eucharist" (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican; from the Greek for "giving thanks") and, for the Orthodox service as a whole, "the Divine Liturgy." The Didache and Justin Martyr's First Apology 66 are among the earliest accounts of how the meal and its prayers came to be arranged.

a: One is hungry, and another is drunk.
t: Hungry and drunk: the abuse of the meal
p: The poor, hungry after work, found little left. The rich were already drunk.
b: The word for "drunk" (methyei) is plain and strong; Paul means it. At a Roman dinner party the host often served guests differently by rank. One reconstruction pictures the scene this way: the better-off began without waiting for those who had to work late, often the poorer members, slaves and day laborers. That is one reconstruction. Others picture separate courses or portions by rank; Paul's phrase "takes his own supper ahead" fits either. The offense was not only greed. It broke the very sign of the Supper, which is one loaf, one body (10:17).

a: what I also handed on to you
p: Paul uses the technical words for passing on a tradition. This is the earliest written account of the Last Supper.
b: "Received" and "handed on" (parelabon, paredoka) are the words for passing on a teaching in Jewish and Greek schools; Paul uses them again for the creed in 15:3. "From the Lord" probably means that the tradition goes back to Jesus through those who were there, not necessarily a private revelation, though some take it as a direct word (compare Galatians 1:11-12). This letter was written during Paul's stay in Ephesus, usually dated between AD 53 and 57, before any Gospel, so it is the earliest written account of the Last Supper. Luke's account (Luke 22:19-20) is closest to Paul's; Mark and Matthew differ in detail. Some argue that the words come from an Aramaic original.

a: the night he was handed over
p: The Greek verb is the same as in 11:23's "handed on" and in Romans 8:32. It is not only about Judas.
b: Paredideto is a form of paradidomi, "hand over," the verb the site renders the same way in Romans (1:24; 4:25; 8:32). The KJV and many translations use "betrayed," which fits Judas (Mark 14:10-11). But the same verb says that God handed over his own Son (Romans 8:32), and that Jesus was handed over for our trespasses (Romans 4:25), where no betrayer is in view. So Paul may include Judas's act, the Father's will and the Son's own giving (Galatians 2:20 says he gave himself for Paul). The word is also the one for "handing on" the tradition, which may be a deliberate play: Jesus was handed over; the story is handed on.

a: This is my body, which is for you.
t: "This is my body": the question of the words
p: Paul has the words that start every debate about the Supper. The churches read "is" in different ways.
b: Paul's words are shorter than in Matthew and Mark: "This is my body, which is for you." Luke 22:19 has "given for you." The question is what "is" means: literal (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran), spiritual presence (Reformed, Anglican), or sign and memorial (Zwingli, Baptist and others). Some argue that the Aramaic Jesus spoke could say this without any word for "is," so that the question is not decided by "is" alone; this is contested, since Aramaic has ways to join two nouns, and some think the meal was spoken in Hebrew. "Which is for you" points to his death as a sacrifice for others. Some argue that Isaiah 53 is in the background of "for" (hyper); not everyone agrees. The cards at Matthew 26:26 and Luke 22:19 give the churches' views.

a: Do this to remember me.
p: "To remember" does not mean only to think about. In Jewish thought it means to bring the past into the present.
b: Anamnesis ("remembrance") is a loaded word. In the Old Testament, to "remember" can mean to act on what is remembered: God "remembered Noah" (Genesis 8:1). At the Passover, a family remembered the exodus as something they shared in (Exodus 12:14; 13:8). Some argue that "do this so that God may remember me" is the Aramaic sense: the meal calls God to remember the Messiah and bring his kingdom. Catholic and Orthodox teaching hold that the Eucharist makes the one sacrifice present (the Catechism, §1362-1367); Reformed and Baptist teaching hold that it is a memorial of a finished work. The Luke 22:19 card gives each church in full.

a: the new covenant, made in my blood
p: Jesus names the "new covenant" promised in Jeremiah 31. Paul and Luke are the only ones to use the phrase.
b: The phrase "new covenant" comes from Jeremiah 31:31-34, which this site renders as a covenant God will make with Israel and Judah, written on their hearts, with sins forgiven. Jesus' cup uses it; Matthew and Mark have "covenant" only. Luke and Paul have "the new covenant." The covenant at Sinai was sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8), and Jesus links his death to both. How the new covenant relates to Israel is debated (supersession, fulfillment, or a covenant opened to Gentiles; see Hebrews 8). Paul himself still holds to God's promises to Israel (Romans 11:29).

a: announce the Lord's death
t: "Until he comes": the Supper looks forward
p: The Supper is also a statement about the future. It looks back to the cross and ahead to the return.
b: The Greek verb katangellete can be read as a command ("announce!") or a statement. Most take it as a statement: eating is itself a way of announcing. "Until he comes" ties the Supper to the church's hope. The cry Maranatha ("Our Lord, come") of 16:22 belongs to the same meal in the Didache, where the eucharistic prayers end with it (Didache 10:6). Eating the bread is not an end in itself; it is looking toward the day Jesus spoke of, when he would drink it new in the kingdom (Mark 14:25). The Orthodox liturgy and others make this a central theme.

a: in an unworthy way
p: Paul's word describes the manner of eating. It is not about the person's moral rank.
b: Anaxios is an adverb: "in an unworthy manner." Paul does not say "unworthy persons" may not eat (no one is worthy). In the setting of 11:17-22 the unworthy manner is eating without regard for the poor, without waiting, with drunkenness. Later church practice often read it as personal sin or lack of faith, which led to fasts and confession before Communion, and sometimes to people avoiding the Supper. "Answerable for the body and blood" (Greek enochos, "liable," often rendered "guilty") means answerable for a wrong done to them, much as someone insulting a king's portrait insults the king. The Byzantine text adds "unworthily" again in 11:29 (see the variant).

a: if he does not discern the body
t: "Discerning the body": the bread, or the church?
p: "The body" may mean the bread, the church, or both. The meaning decides what the sin is.
b: Diakrino means "tell apart, judge rightly." Which "body" is meant? (1) The eucharistic body: failing to recognize the bread as Christ's body (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran readings). (2) The church: failing to recognize the other members as one body, as 10:17 and chapter 12 suggest. (3) Both at once, since for Paul the two are linked (10:16-17). The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which has no "unworthily" and no "of the Lord" here (see the variant), so the verse reads more sharply as a charge about "the body." The card below gives how the churches read the passage.

a: quite a few have fallen asleep
p: Paul says some in Corinth were sick and some had died because of the way they ate. Was this punishment?
b: "Fallen asleep" is Paul's usual way of speaking of Christian death (15:6, 18, 20). He says "many" are weak and sick but uses a smaller word (hikanoi, "a fair number") for the dead, so the Plain says "quite a few." He connects the weakness, sickness and deaths in Corinth with the abuse of the meal. This is hard to read without a lot of discussion. Views: (1) God's actual discipline, as the next verses say (11:32). (2) A warning given with some irony, not a rule that sickness is always punishment (Job and John 9:1-3 are counter-examples). (3) Natural results: sick and hungry people who went without food, or the spread of illness at crowded meals. The text says they were disciplined "so that we will not be condemned along with the world." The discipline is not damnation.

a: we are being disciplined
p: God's judgment now is a teacher's correction. It differs from the final verdict.
b: Paideuo is the verb for raising and training a child, and it can include punishment (Hebrews 12:5-11, from Proverbs 3:11-12). Paul separates this discipline of believers from the condemnation (katakrino) of the world. A person under the Lord's correction is still his. Churches draw different lessons. Reformed teachers read it as showing that God's people can be chastised but not lost (Westminster Confession 17.3); Catholic teaching speaks of temporal punishment that remains even after forgiveness (Catechism 1472); Wesleyans hold that people can still fall away. The verse itself says only what the discipline is for.

a: wait for each other
p: Paul's verb can mean wait for or receive. Both fit the problem of the meal.
b: The verb is ekdechesthe. Most take it as "wait for" (compare 16:11 and Hebrews 10:13): the rich must not start before the poor arrive. Some take it as "receive, welcome," the sense of receiving guests, which also fits a meal at which each person grabbed his own supper (11:21). The two senses meet in the same action: do not begin without the others. The Plain says "wait for each other."

a: I will set the other matters in order when I come
p: Paul leaves some questions for a visit. We do not know what they were.
b: Paul often says he will deal with things in person (4:19; 16:2-8; 2 Corinthians 13:1-2). "The other matters" could refer to the rest of the Supper's practices, or to further problems in worship. His plan to come is real: he is writing from Ephesus on his third journey, and he stays in Corinth for three months after his plans change (Acts 20:2-3). Whatever he meant to set in order is gone from our record. The Lord's Supper then developed with little else from the New Testament, which is why the Didache, Justin and the later liturgies are so important to the debates about its form.
